claims.claim: Michael Swanwick judges that From Elfland to Poughkeepsie holds up extremely well thirty-seven years after publication and would still be a good starting place for someone learning to write fantasy.
claims.quote: Yes, the essay holds up extremely well

claims.claim: Michael Swanwick argues that the essay's central conceit, that Poughkeepsie stands in for everything fantasy is not, has been disproved by Rachel Pollack's Unquenchable Fire, a core fantasy set in Poughkeepsie.
Le Guin, quoted by John Pyle from From Elfland to Poughkeepsie, wrote that a writer may use all the trappings of fantasy without ever actually imagining anything.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), quoted in John Pyle, 23 November 2012

claims.claim: Alessandro Amenta finds that the Polish translator Stanislaw Baranczak, while reproducing the novel's different linguistic registers, is inclined to elevate the tone of the phrase by an ennobling strategy accompanied by expansion and amplification.
claims.source: Alessandro Amenta, Kwartalnik Neofilologiczny LXX 2/2023, p. 282
claims.quote: inclined to elevate the tone of the phrase

claims.claim: Alessandro Amenta states that different linguistic registers are employed in A Wizard of Earthsea and that the Polish translator generally respects and reproduces them.
claims.quote: generally respects and reproduces the different linguistic registers

claims.claim: Alessandro Amenta reports that Le Guin's neologisms for plants, animals, fantastic creatures and objects - perriot, corly, gebbeth, pellawi, otak, harrekki - are usually borrowed into Polish without any adaptation.
claims.source: Alessandro Amenta, Kwartalnik Neofilologiczny LXX 2/2023, p. 281

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Philip Chase from From Elfland to Poughkeepsie, wrote that if you remove the style all you have left is a synopsis of the plot.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), quoted in Philip Chase (video), 16 November 2021
claims.quote: if you remove the style all you have left is a synopsis
claims.page: quotation of the essay in the second half of the video

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Philip Chase, wrote that in fantasy there is only a construct built in a void with every joint and seam and nail exposed.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), quoted in Philip Chase (video), 16 November 2021
claims.quote: a construct built in a void with every joint and seam

claims.claim: A speaker on Tooky's Mag paraphrases Le Guin as holding that in fantasy every time a character speaks the speech is itself an act of worldbuilding, because the writer cannot rely on shared history.
claims.source: Tooky's Mag, 'How Le Guin Wrote Fantasy' (video podcast), 12 April 2024
claims.quote: every time a character speaks is itself an active World building

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Kate Nepveu, calls two closing sentences of straightforward narrative description full of rapid reversals and says they are like drumbeats.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings', quoted in Kate Nepveu, LiveJournal, 4 June 2006
claims.page: analysis of the closing sentences of 'Fog on the Barrow-Downs'

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Mary Anne Mohanraj, wrote in her 1987 bracketed revision that the English generic singular pronoun was they, them, their until the sixteenth century and should be restored to the written language, letting the pedants and pundits squeak and gibber in the streets.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, bracketed 1987 commentary in 'Is Gender Necessary? Redux' (Dancing at the Edge of the World), quoted in Mary Anne Mohanraj, Reactor, 1 November 2018
claims.quote: let the pedants and pundits squeak and gibber in the streets

claims.claim: Le Guin told Paul Morton that in writing, if you do not have to mention the doorknob you do not, unlike film where every visual object must be designed.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by Paul Morton, The Millions, 31 January 2013
claims.quote: if you don't have to mention the doorknob you don't

claims.claim: Le Guin said of rereading The Lathe of Heaven that she would cut it, because the characters talk too much and explain things too much.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by Paul Morton, The Millions, 31 January 2013
claims.quote: They talk too much. They explain things too much.

claims.claim: Le Guin said she does not write dialogue the way Hemingway writes Spanish-accented English in For Whom the Bell Tolls, and that she finds it a little affected and foolish.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by Paul Morton, The Millions, 31 January 2013
claims.quote: I find it a little affected and foolish

claims.claim: Le Guin told Jonathan White that she believes words are acts and that writers must therefore be held responsible for what their words do.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by Jonathan White, 'Coming Back From the Silence'
claims.quote: If you believe that words are acts, as I do
claims.page: section on language as a tool of forgetting
